subject: physiology
prompt: During quiet inspiration in a healthy adult, which action is the principal cause of the increase in thoracic volume?

options.text: Contraction of the abdominal rectus muscles
Contraction and downward movement of the diaphragm
Contraction of the internal intercostal muscles
Passive recoil of the lungs

explanation: Diaphragmatic contraction pulls the lower surfaces of the lungs downward and is the main driver of normal quiet inspiration.

distractorExplanations.A: Abdominal contraction pushes the diaphragm upward during forceful expiration.
distractorExplanations.C: Internal intercostal contraction helps lower the rib cage during expiration.
distractorExplanations.D: Passive elastic recoil primarily produces quiet expiration, not inspiration.

learningObjective: Identify the principal muscle action responsible for quiet inspiration.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: A healthy adult begins a quiet inspiration with an open glottis. Pressures are measured relative to atmospheric pressure. Which combination is expected while air is flowing into the lungs?

options.text: Positive alveolar pressure and less negative pleural pressure
Positive alveolar pressure and more negative pleural pressure
Negative alveolar pressure and positive pleural pressure
Slightly negative alveolar pressure and more negative pleural pressure

explanation: Inspiratory expansion makes pleural pressure more negative and lowers alveolar pressure slightly below atmospheric pressure. The alveolar-to-atmospheric pressure difference drives inward airflow.

distractorExplanations.A: Positive alveolar pressure would drive air outward; pleural pressure normally becomes more negative during inspiration.
distractorExplanations.B: More negative pleural pressure is appropriate, but positive alveolar pressure would oppose inward airflow.
distractorExplanations.C: Quiet inspiration does not make pleural pressure positive; it becomes more negative.

learningObjective: Relate inspiratory airflow to alveolar and pleural pressure changes.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: At one instant during inspiration, alveolar pressure is -1 cm H2O and pleural pressure is -7 cm H2O, both relative to atmosphere. What is the transpulmonary pressure?

options.text: +6 cm H2O
-6 cm H2O
+8 cm H2O
-8 cm H2O

explanation: Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar pressure minus pleural pressure: -1 - (-7) = +6 cm H2O. It is the distending pressure across the lung.

distractorExplanations.B: This reverses the subtraction and gives pleural minus alveolar pressure.
distractorExplanations.C: Adding the absolute values ignores the signed pressure difference.
distractorExplanations.D: Adding the two signed pressures does not calculate transpulmonary pressure.

learningObjective: Calculate transpulmonary pressure using signed pressure measurements.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: After sufficient time for equilibration, increasing transpulmonary pressure from 5 to 7 cm H2O increases the volume of both lungs by 400 mL. What is their compliance over this interval?

options.text: 100 mL/cm H2O
400 mL/cm H2O
200 mL/cm H2O
800 mL/cm H2O

explanation: Compliance equals change in lung volume divided by change in transpulmonary pressure. Here, 400 mL / (7 - 5) cm H2O = 200 mL/cm H2O.

distractorExplanations.A: A value of 100 would require a 4 cm H2O pressure change for this volume change.
distractorExplanations.B: This uses the volume change without dividing by the 2 cm H2O pressure change.
distractorExplanations.D: Multiplying volume change by pressure change is not compliance.

learningObjective: Calculate static lung compliance from an equilibrated pressure-volume change.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: In an isolated-lung experiment, substantially less transpulmonary pressure is needed to produce a given volume increase when the lung is filled with saline rather than air. What best explains this finding?

options.text: Saline removes all collagen and elastin from the lung
Saline strengthens the recoil produced by alveolar surface tension
Saline eliminates the alveolar air-fluid interface and its surface tension contribution
Saline causes the chest wall muscles to contract more strongly

explanation: A saline-filled lung lacks the air-fluid interface responsible for much of the recoil of an air-filled lung. Tissue elasticity remains, but the surface tension contribution is removed.

distractorExplanations.A: Saline filling does not remove the lung's elastic tissue; tissue recoil is still present.
distractorExplanations.B: The surface tension contribution is removed, not strengthened, when there is no air-fluid interface.
distractorExplanations.D: This is an isolated lung; chest wall muscle activity cannot explain its pressure-volume relation.

learningObjective: Distinguish tissue elasticity from alveolar surface tension as sources of lung recoil.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: A premature infant has inadequate pulmonary surfactant. Which change most directly explains the increased tendency of the alveoli to collapse?

options.text: Increased surface tension in the alveolar lining fluid
Decreased elastic recoil of the air-filled lungs
Increased ease of lung expansion at a given pressure
Loss of the normal surface-tension-raising action of surfactant

explanation: Surfactant, secreted by type II alveolar epithelial cells, lowers surface tension. Its deficiency raises the surface tension force tending to collapse the alveoli and makes inflation more difficult.

distractorExplanations.B: Surfactant deficiency increases the surface tension component of recoil rather than decreasing it.
distractorExplanations.C: Deficiency makes expansion harder, not easier, for a given distending pressure.
distractorExplanations.D: Normal surfactant lowers surface tension; it does not raise it.

learningObjective: Explain how surfactant deficiency alters alveolar stability and inflation.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: Two idealized spherical alveoli have identical, constant lining-fluid surface tension. Alveolus X has half the radius of alveolus Y. Using the book's relationship P = 2T/r, how does the pressure tending to collapse X compare with that for Y?

options.text: One-quarter as great
One-half as great
The same
Twice as great

explanation: With surface tension held constant, collapse pressure is inversely proportional to radius. Halving the radius doubles 2T/r; real surfactant behavior is intentionally excluded by the stated assumption.

distractorExplanations.A: The stated relationship contains the first power of radius in the denominator, not its square.
distractorExplanations.B: Halving radius increases rather than decreases pressure when surface tension is unchanged.
distractorExplanations.C: Equal surface tension does not produce equal pressure when the radii differ.

learningObjective: Apply the inverse relationship between alveolar radius and collapse pressure with surface tension fixed.

subject: physiology
subtopic: Work of breathing and airway resistance
prompt: During an episode of bronchial smooth-muscle constriction, a patient must generate a larger pressure difference to maintain the same airflow. Which component of the work of inspiration is most directly increased?

options.text: Work required to overcome lung tissue elasticity alone
Airway resistance work
Work required to increase alveolar diffusion capacity
Work required to transport oxygen bound to hemoglobin

explanation: Narrowing the airway increases resistance to airflow. The additional pressure needed to move air through that resistance increases airway resistance work.

distractorExplanations.A: Elastic work concerns expansion against recoil; the specified change is airway narrowing.
distractorExplanations.C: Diffusion across the respiratory membrane is not a mechanical work component of inspiration.
distractorExplanations.D: Hemoglobin transport is not one of the mechanical work components of breathing.

learningObjective: Identify the work-of-breathing component increased by bronchoconstriction.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: A student measures the volume of gas remaining in the lungs at the end of a normal, unforced expiration. Which volume or capacity has been measured?

options.text: Functional residual capacity
Residual volume
Inspiratory capacity
Vital capacity

explanation: Functional residual capacity is the gas remaining after a normal expiration. It is the sum of expiratory reserve volume and residual volume.

distractorExplanations.B: Residual volume remains after the most forceful expiration, not merely a normal expiration.
distractorExplanations.C: Inspiratory capacity is the volume that can be inspired from the normal end-expiratory level.
distractorExplanations.D: Vital capacity is the maximum exhaled volume after maximal inspiration.

learningObjective: Recognize the definition and components of functional residual capacity.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: Which quantity cannot be measured directly with a simple spirometer that records only air entering and leaving the mouth?

options.text: Tidal volume
Expiratory reserve volume
Residual volume
Vital capacity

explanation: Residual volume cannot be exhaled into the spirometer. Capacities containing residual volume also require another method, such as helium dilution, rather than simple spirometry alone.

distractorExplanations.A: Tidal volume is the inspired or expired volume of an ordinary breath and can be recorded.
distractorExplanations.B: Expiratory reserve volume is the extra volume exhaled after a normal expiration and can be recorded.
distractorExplanations.D: Vital capacity is an exhalable volume from maximal inspiration to maximal expiration and can be recorded.

learningObjective: Distinguish exhalable lung volumes from volumes inaccessible to simple spirometry.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: A subject has a tidal volume of 500 mL, an inspiratory reserve volume of 3000 mL, an expiratory reserve volume of 1000 mL, and a residual volume of 1200 mL. What is the vital capacity?
explanation: Vital capacity equals inspiratory reserve volume + tidal volume + expiratory reserve volume: 3000 + 500 + 1000 = 4500 mL. Residual volume is not included.

distractorExplanations.A: 3500 mL is the inspiratory capacity, which omits expiratory reserve volume.
distractorExplanations.C: 4700 mL incorrectly substitutes residual volume for expiratory reserve volume.
distractorExplanations.D: 5700 mL is total lung capacity, which includes residual volume.

learningObjective: Calculate vital capacity and distinguish it from other lung capacities.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: At the end of a normal expiration, a subject is connected to a closed spirometer containing 3.0 L of gas with 10% helium. After complete mixing, helium concentration is 6%. Assume no leaks, negligible helium absorption, and correction for oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide removal. What is the functional residual capacity?
explanation: FRC = initial spirometer volume x (initial helium fraction/final helium fraction - 1). Thus FRC = 3.0 x (10/6 - 1) = 2.0 L; the final combined gas volume is 5.0 L.

distractorExplanations.A: This does not conserve the initial helium quantity of 0.30 L across the combined volume.
distractorExplanations.B: Multiplying the fractional concentration fall by 3.0 L does not account for dilution into the added lung volume.
distractorExplanations.C: 5.0 L is the combined final volume of spirometer plus lung gas, not the lung volume alone.

learningObjective: Calculate functional residual capacity using a closed-circuit helium dilution experiment.

subject: physiology
prompt: A subject breathes 12 times/min with a tidal volume of 500 mL and a physiological dead space of 150 mL per breath. What is the alveolar ventilation?

options.text: 1.8 L/min
6.0 L/min
4.2 L/min
7.8 L/min

explanation: Alveolar ventilation = respiratory rate x (tidal volume - physiological dead space). Therefore, 12 x (500 - 150) = 4200 mL/min = 4.2 L/min.

distractorExplanations.A: 1.8 L/min is dead-space ventilation: 12 x 150 mL.
distractorExplanations.B: 6.0 L/min is total minute ventilation and includes dead-space ventilation.
distractorExplanations.D: 7.8 L/min adds rather than subtracts dead-space volume from each tidal breath.

learningObjective: Calculate alveolar ventilation after excluding physiological dead space.

subject: physiology
prompt: A subject changes from 12 breaths/min at 500 mL per breath to 24 breaths/min at 250 mL per breath. Physiological dead space stays at 150 mL per breath. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Minute ventilation and alveolar ventilation both remain unchanged
Minute ventilation is unchanged, but alveolar ventilation falls from 4.2 to 2.4 L/min
Minute ventilation doubles, but alveolar ventilation is unchanged
Minute ventilation is unchanged, but alveolar ventilation rises from 4.2 to 6.0 L/min

explanation: Minute ventilation is 6.0 L/min in both patterns. Alveolar ventilation falls from 12 x 350 = 4200 mL/min to 24 x 100 = 2400 mL/min because more breaths repeatedly ventilate dead space.

distractorExplanations.A: Equal minute ventilation does not imply equal alveolar ventilation when tidal volume and rate change.
distractorExplanations.C: Doubling rate while halving tidal volume leaves minute ventilation unchanged.
distractorExplanations.D: 6.0 L/min is the total minute ventilation; subtracting dead space gives only 2.4 L/min for the second pattern.

learningObjective: Compare effective alveolar ventilation during deep-slow and shallow-rapid breathing.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 39: Pulmonary Circulation, Pulmonary Edema, and Pleural Fluid
prompt: A small group of alveoli becomes poorly ventilated, while ventilation elsewhere remains normal. What local vascular response helps improve the overall matching of pulmonary blood flow to ventilation?

options.text: Dilation of arteries supplying the hypoxic alveoli
Constriction of vessels supplying only the well-ventilated alveoli
Equal dilation of all pulmonary arterioles
Constriction of small pulmonary arteries supplying the hypoxic alveoli

explanation: Low alveolar oxygen causes local pulmonary vasoconstriction. This diverts blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli toward regions with better ventilation.

distractorExplanations.A: Dilation would direct more blood to poorly ventilated alveoli and worsen matching.
distractorExplanations.B: Constriction in well-ventilated regions would divert flow away from the regions best able to oxygenate it.
distractorExplanations.C: A uniform response would not selectively redirect blood away from the hypoxic region.

learningObjective: Explain how local alveolar hypoxia redistributes pulmonary blood flow.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 39: Pulmonary Circulation, Pulmonary Edema, and Pleural Fluid
prompt: In a region of lung, alveolar pressure is 10 mm Hg. Local pulmonary arterial pressure varies from 15 mm Hg in systole to 5 mm Hg in diastole, and pulmonary venous pressure stays below 10 mm Hg. Which blood-flow pattern is expected?

options.text: Zone 2 flow: flow during systole but interruption during diastole
Zone 1 flow: no flow throughout the entire cardiac cycle
Zone 3 flow: continuous flow throughout the cardiac cycle
Continuous reverse flow from pulmonary veins to pulmonary arteries

explanation: Arterial pressure exceeds alveolar pressure in systole but falls below it in diastole. This is zone 2, in which alveolar compression interrupts flow when intravascular pressure becomes too low.

distractorExplanations.B: Zone 1 requires alveolar pressure to exceed arterial pressure throughout the cycle, which is not true in systole here.
distractorExplanations.C: Continuous zone 3 flow requires vascular pressures to remain sufficient to prevent alveolar compression throughout the cycle.
distractorExplanations.D: The given arterial-to-venous pressure relationship does not support continuous reverse flow.

learningObjective: Classify pulmonary blood-flow zones from alveolar and vascular pressures.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 39: Pulmonary Circulation, Pulmonary Edema, and Pleural Fluid
prompt: During strenuous exercise, pulmonary blood flow increases several-fold but mean pulmonary arterial pressure rises relatively little. What is the principal explanation?

options.text: A proportional increase in pulmonary vascular resistance
Recruitment and distension of pulmonary capillaries
Diversion of most right ventricular output into the bronchial circulation
Generalized closure of upper-lung capillaries

explanation: Exercise opens additional pulmonary capillaries and distends vessels already carrying blood. The resulting fall in resistance accommodates a large flow increase with a limited pressure rise.

distractorExplanations.A: An increase in resistance would require a larger, not smaller, pressure rise for the increased flow.
distractorExplanations.C: The bronchial circulation is a small systemic circuit and does not receive most right ventricular output.
distractorExplanations.D: Exercise improves upper-lung perfusion rather than closing its capillaries.

learningObjective: Explain how pulmonary vascular recruitment and distension accommodate exercise blood flow.

prompt: A catheter tip is advanced until it wedges in a small pulmonary arterial branch. Under the usual conditions described in the text, changes in the measured wedge pressure most closely estimate changes in which pressure?

options.text: Aortic systolic pressure
Right ventricular systolic pressure
Left atrial pressure
Pleural pressure alone

explanation: Pulmonary wedge pressure provides an indirect estimate of left atrial pressure and its changes. The text notes that the wedge value can be slightly higher, so the two are not assumed to be numerically identical.

distractorExplanations.A: The wedge measurement is obtained in the pulmonary circuit, not the aorta.
distractorExplanations.B: Occluding the small arterial branch removes direct transmission of the upstream right ventricular systolic pressure to the distal measurement.
distractorExplanations.D: Pleural pressure can influence thoracic pressures, but wedge pressure is not a measurement of pleural pressure alone.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 39: Pulmonary Circulation, Pulmonary Edema, and Pleural Fluid
prompt: A sudden marked rise in left atrial pressure is followed by pulmonary interstitial edema. Assume that plasma protein concentration and capillary permeability have not initially changed. Which alteration most directly drives fluid out of the pulmonary capillaries?

options.text: Increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
Increased plasma colloid osmotic pressure
Decreased interstitial protein concentration
Decreased pulmonary capillary filtration pressure

explanation: Raised left atrial pressure can raise pulmonary venous and capillary pressure. The increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure favors outward filtration and can overwhelm fluid removal.

distractorExplanations.B: Higher plasma oncotic pressure would oppose filtration, and protein concentration is specified as unchanged.
distractorExplanations.C: Lower interstitial protein would reduce outward oncotic pull rather than explain increased filtration.
distractorExplanations.D: Edema in this setting follows increased outward filtration pressure, not a decrease.

learningObjective: Explain hydrostatic pulmonary edema caused by an acute rise in left-sided filling pressure.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 39: Pulmonary Circulation, Pulmonary Edema, and Pleural Fluid
prompt: Pulmonary capillary membranes are damaged by an inhaled noxious gas. Left atrial pressure remains normal, but protein-rich fluid accumulates in the lung interstitium and alveoli. Which mechanism best explains the edema?

options.text: An isolated rise in plasma protein concentration
A decrease in capillary permeability to protein
An isolated reduction in pulmonary venous pressure
Increased capillary permeability with leakage of protein and fluid

explanation: Capillary membrane injury allows plasma proteins and fluid to escape into the interstitium and alveoli. This can produce pulmonary edema without a primary increase in left atrial pressure.

distractorExplanations.A: Increasing plasma protein concentration would strengthen the inward oncotic force and would not explain protein leakage.
distractorExplanations.B: Reduced permeability would limit protein escape rather than produce protein-rich edema.
distractorExplanations.C: Lower venous pressure generally reduces hydrostatic filtration and does not explain the injured membrane.

learningObjective: Distinguish increased-permeability edema from edema caused by elevated vascular pressure.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 39: Pulmonary Circulation, Pulmonary Edema, and Pleural Fluid
prompt: Compared with an abrupt rise, a slowly developing elevation of pulmonary capillary pressure may be tolerated with less edema at the same final pressure. Which adaptation described in the text contributes to this difference?

options.text: Complete disappearance of pulmonary capillary filtration
Conversion of the pulmonary circulation into a high-resistance circuit
Marked expansion of pulmonary lymphatic drainage capacity
Loss of the lymphatics' ability to carry interstitial protein

explanation: With chronic pressure elevation, pulmonary lymphatics can greatly increase their capacity to remove interstitial fluid. This raises the safety margin against edema compared with an abrupt pressure increase.

distractorExplanations.A: Filtration continues; improved removal helps balance it.
distractorExplanations.B: An increase in pulmonary resistance is not the lymphatic adaptation described and does not itself remove excess fluid.
distractorExplanations.D: Impaired protein removal would favor, not protect against, interstitial fluid accumulation.

learningObjective: Explain why chronic lymphatic adaptation can increase resistance to pulmonary edema.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 39: Pulmonary Circulation, Pulmonary Edema, and Pleural Fluid
prompt: A patient develops a pleural effusion after obstruction of lymphatic drainage from the pleural cavity. Which normal process has most directly been impaired?

options.text: Movement of oxygen from alveoli into pulmonary capillaries
Removal of excess pleural fluid through lymphatic openings
Secretion of surfactant into the alveolar lining fluid
Transport of carbon dioxide as bicarbonate in blood

explanation: Pleural lymphatics normally remove excess fluid from the potential space between the pleural surfaces. Blocking this drainage permits fluid to accumulate as an effusion.

distractorExplanations.A: Alveolar gas diffusion is a different process from drainage of fluid in the pleural cavity.
distractorExplanations.C: Surfactant secretion occurs within the alveoli and does not remove excess pleural fluid.
distractorExplanations.D: Bicarbonate transport concerns blood gas carriage, not pleural fluid turnover.

learningObjective: Describe the role of lymphatic drainage in maintaining a small pleural fluid volume.

prompt: A person breathes air with an oxygen fraction of 0.21 at a barometric pressure of 500 mm Hg. Inspired gas becomes fully saturated with water vapor at 37 degrees C, where water vapor pressure is 47 mm Hg. Before alveolar gas exchange, what is the approximate oxygen partial pressure of this humidified inspired gas?

options.text: 58 mm Hg
105 mm Hg
95 mm Hg
149 mm Hg

explanation: Water vapor occupies 47 mm Hg of the total pressure. Humidified inspired PO2 = 0.21 x (500 - 47) = 95.13 mm Hg, approximately 95 mm Hg; alveolar exchange is not included in this calculation.

distractorExplanations.A: This subtracts all 47 mm Hg from the dry oxygen partial pressure rather than applying oxygen fraction to the remaining dry-gas pressure.
distractorExplanations.B: 105 mm Hg is the dry-air oxygen partial pressure, 0.21 x 500, before humidification.
distractorExplanations.D: Approximately 149 mm Hg applies to humidified room air at sea-level pressure, not at 500 mm Hg.

learningObjective: Calculate inspired oxygen partial pressure after humidification at reduced barometric pressure.

prompt: At steady state, alveolar PCO2 is 40 mm Hg. Alveolar ventilation is then doubled while carbon dioxide production remains unchanged, and a new steady state is reached. What is the expected alveolar PCO2?

options.text: 20 mm Hg
40 mm Hg
60 mm Hg
80 mm Hg

explanation: At unchanged CO2 production, alveolar PCO2 varies inversely with alveolar ventilation. Doubling ventilation therefore halves PCO2 from 40 to 20 mm Hg.

distractorExplanations.B: PCO2 would remain unchanged only if CO2 production rose proportionally with ventilation.
distractorExplanations.C: An increase in ventilation at fixed production lowers, rather than raises, alveolar PCO2.
distractorExplanations.D: 80 mm Hg would follow halving, not doubling, ventilation under these assumptions.

learningObjective: Predict steady-state alveolar PCO2 after a change in alveolar ventilation.

prompt: For a particular gas, respiratory membrane thickness doubles and available surface area falls to half its initial value. The diffusion coefficient and partial pressure difference remain unchanged. What fraction of the original diffusion rate is expected?

The same
Twice
One-quarter

explanation: Diffusion rate is proportional to surface area and inversely proportional to thickness. The combined factor is (1/2)/2 = 1/4 of the original rate.

prompt: Under comparable conditions, carbon dioxide can cross the respiratory membrane at a much higher rate than oxygen for the same partial pressure difference. What chiefly explains this property?

options.text: Carbon dioxide has a lower molecular weight than oxygen
Carbon dioxide is much more soluble in the membrane and tissue fluid
Carbon dioxide requires no partial pressure difference to diffuse
Oxygen is unable to dissolve in the respiratory membrane

explanation: The diffusion coefficient depends strongly on gas solubility and inversely on the square root of molecular weight. CO2's much greater solubility makes its diffusion rate about 20 times that of O2 for a given pressure difference.

distractorExplanations.A: CO2 has a higher, not lower, molecular weight; its greater solubility dominates this comparison.
distractorExplanations.C: Net CO2 diffusion still requires a partial pressure difference.
distractorExplanations.D: Oxygen does dissolve and diffuse through the membrane, but less readily than CO2 for the same pressure gradient.

learningObjective: Explain the high diffusion coefficient of carbon dioxide relative to oxygen.

prompt: Why is a small test concentration of carbon monoxide useful for measuring the lung's diffusing capacity?

CO cannot cross the respiratory membrane
CO is not taken up by pulmonary capillary blood
CO partial pressure immediately becomes equal on both sides of the membrane

prompt: An embolus completely stops blood flow to an alveolar unit, but that unit remains ventilated with humidified room air at sea level. After sufficient time, what happens to its alveolar gases?

PO2 falls to zero while PCO2 rises continuously
They necessarily remain at normal alveolar PO2 and PCO2

chapter: Chapter 41: Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide in Blood and Tissue Fluids
prompt: A blood sample contains 10 g hemoglobin/dL, and hemoglobin is 90% saturated with oxygen. Assume each gram of hemoglobin binds 1.34 mL O2 at full saturation and ignore dissolved oxygen. What is its hemoglobin-bound oxygen content?

options.text: 9.0 mL O2/dL
12.1 mL O2/dL
13.4 mL O2/dL
20.1 mL O2/dL

explanation: Bound oxygen content = hemoglobin concentration x oxygen capacity per gram x fractional saturation. Thus 10 x 1.34 x 0.90 = 12.06, or approximately 12.1 mL O2/dL.

distractorExplanations.A: Multiplying hemoglobin concentration by saturation alone omits its oxygen-binding capacity per gram.
distractorExplanations.C: 13.4 mL/dL is the capacity at 100% saturation, not the content at 90% saturation.
distractorExplanations.D: 20.1 mL/dL would be the full-saturation capacity of 15 g/dL hemoglobin, not the stated sample.

learningObjective: Calculate hemoglobin-bound oxygen content from hemoglobin concentration and saturation.

prompt: Arterial blood entering a tissue contains 20 mL O2/dL, and venous blood leaving it contains 15 mL O2/dL. Using oxygen content rather than partial pressure, what is the oxygen utilization coefficient?
explanation: The tissue removes 20 - 15 = 5 mL O2/dL. The utilization coefficient is the fraction of delivered oxygen extracted: 5/20 x 100 = 25%.

distractorExplanations.A: 5 is the absolute content difference in mL/dL, not the percentage extracted.
distractorExplanations.B: 20 is the incoming oxygen content, not its extracted fraction.
distractorExplanations.C: 75% is the fraction remaining in venous blood, not the fraction used by the tissue.

learningObjective: Calculate the fraction of delivered oxygen extracted by a tissue.

prompt: Why does a moderate fall in alveolar PO2 from about 104 to 60 mm Hg produce a relatively small fall in hemoglobin oxygen saturation, assuming normal hemoglobin and adequate equilibration?

options.text: Hemoglobin binds oxygen independently of oxygen partial pressure
Dissolved oxygen completely replaces hemoglobin-bound oxygen
This pressure range lies largely on the upper, relatively flat portion of the dissociation curve
Hemoglobin saturation rises whenever alveolar PO2 falls

explanation: The upper part of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is relatively flat. Hemoglobin therefore remains substantially saturated despite a moderate reduction in alveolar and end-capillary PO2.

distractorExplanations.A: Oxygen binding depends on PO2; the small change reflects the curve's shape, not pressure independence.
distractorExplanations.B: Dissolved oxygen remains a small component under these conditions and does not replace hemoglobin carriage.
distractorExplanations.D: Saturation decreases as PO2 falls when the curve is otherwise unchanged.

learningObjective: Explain the oxygen-loading reserve provided by the plateau of the hemoglobin dissociation curve.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 41: Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide in Blood and Tissue Fluids
prompt: Blood passes through a metabolically active tissue where CO2 and hydrogen ion concentrations increase. At a given tissue PO2, how does this change affect hemoglobin?

options.text: It shifts the oxygen dissociation curve rightward and promotes oxygen release
It shifts the curve leftward and promotes oxygen release
It shifts the curve rightward and increases oxygen affinity
It leaves oxygen affinity unchanged because only PO2 can alter binding

explanation: Increased CO2 and H+ shift the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the right, reducing affinity at a given PO2 and enhancing unloading. This is the Bohr effect.

distractorExplanations.B: A left shift raises affinity and tends to impede unloading at a fixed PO2.
distractorExplanations.C: A right shift represents reduced, not increased, oxygen affinity.
distractorExplanations.D: CO2 and pH can alter affinity even when PO2 is held constant.

learningObjective: Apply the Bohr effect to oxygen unloading in active tissues.

subject: physiology

prompt: Two blood samples have the same hemoglobin concentration, PO2, pH, PCO2, and 2,3-BPG concentration. One sample is warmed from 37 to 40 degrees C, as may occur locally in exercising muscle. What is expected in the warmed sample?

options.text: A left shift with greater oxygen saturation at the same PO2
No change because temperature does not affect hemoglobin affinity
An increase in the maximum number of oxygen-binding sites per hemoglobin molecule
A right shift with greater tendency to release oxygen

explanation: Higher temperature shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve rightward. This favors oxygen unloading in warm, active muscle even when other determinants of affinity are held constant.

distractorExplanations.A: Warming causes a right shift, not the left shift associated with greater affinity.
distractorExplanations.B: Temperature is one of the factors that changes the curve independently of PO2.
distractorExplanations.C: Temperature alters affinity over this range, not the number of binding sites on each hemoglobin molecule.

learningObjective: Isolate the effect of increased temperature on hemoglobin oxygen affinity.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 41: Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide in Blood and Tissue Fluids
prompt: After sustained hypoxia, red-cell 2,3-BPG concentration rises. With other factors held constant, how does this change assist tissue oxygen delivery?

options.text: It shifts the dissociation curve leftward so oxygen is held more tightly
It shifts the dissociation curve rightward so oxygen is released at a higher tissue PO2
It converts most oxygen transport from the hemoglobin-bound to the dissolved form
It increases inspired oxygen partial pressure

explanation: An increase in 2,3-BPG shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin curve to the right. The reduced affinity facilitates release of oxygen to tissues at a given PO2.

distractorExplanations.A: A BPG increase causes a right shift, whereas a left shift would favor tighter oxygen binding.
distractorExplanations.C: Hemoglobin remains the principal oxygen carrier; increased BPG changes its affinity.
distractorExplanations.D: An intracellular red-cell metabolite does not change inspired gas pressure.

learningObjective: Explain how increased 2,3-BPG can support oxygen unloading during sustained hypoxia.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 41: Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide in Blood and Tissue Fluids
prompt: After carbon monoxide exposure, a patient has markedly reduced blood oxygen content even though arterial PO2 is near normal. What best explains this combination?

options.text: CO occupies hemoglobin oxygen-binding sites without necessarily reducing dissolved oxygen partial pressure
A normal PO2 proves that hemoglobin-bound oxygen content is normal
CO increases the amount of oxygen that each hemoglobin molecule can carry
CO lowers oxygen content only by preventing oxygen from entering the alveoli

explanation: CO binds strongly at the sites used by oxygen and reduces hemoglobin oxygen-carrying capacity. Blood PO2 can remain normal because partial pressure and hemoglobin-bound oxygen content are different quantities.

distractorExplanations.B: Normal PO2 does not establish normal oxygen content when hemoglobin binding is impaired.
distractorExplanations.C: CO occupies binding sites and reduces, rather than increases, capacity for oxygen.
distractorExplanations.D: The key mechanism described is competition for hemoglobin, not a necessary block to alveolar oxygen entry.

learningObjective: Distinguish arterial oxygen partial pressure from oxygen content in carbon monoxide exposure.

prompt: As blood acquires CO2 in systemic tissue capillaries, carbonic anhydrase promotes bicarbonate formation inside red cells. Which membrane movement normally accompanies this process?

options.text: Bicarbonate enters red cells while chloride leaves
Both bicarbonate and chloride leave red cells together
Bicarbonate leaves red cells while chloride enters
Neither ion crosses the red-cell membrane

explanation: In tissues, CO2 hydration generates bicarbonate in red cells. Bicarbonate moves into plasma through the bicarbonate-chloride exchanger while chloride enters, producing the tissue-side chloride shift.

distractorExplanations.A: This is the reverse direction associated with converting bicarbonate back to CO2 in the lungs.
distractorExplanations.B: The exchanger moves bicarbonate and chloride in opposite directions, not together.
distractorExplanations.D: Membrane exchange is a key step in carrying the large bicarbonate component of CO2 transport.

learningObjective: Predict bicarbonate and chloride movement during systemic carbon dioxide uptake.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 41: Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide in Blood and Tissue Fluids
prompt: During passage through pulmonary capillaries, oxygenation of hemoglobin promotes release of additional CO2. Which explanation describes the Haldane effect?

options.text: Oxygenation increases hemoglobin's capacity to bind CO2 and H+
A rise in CO2 shifts the oxygen dissociation curve rightward
Oxygenated hemoglobin binds less CO2 and releases H+, which helps convert bicarbonate into CO2
Oxygen directly replaces bicarbonate ions in the plasma

explanation: Oxygenation makes hemoglobin less able to carry carbamino CO2 and promotes release of H+. Those H+ ions combine with bicarbonate, facilitating CO2 formation and exhalation.

distractorExplanations.A: Oxygenation reduces these carrying and buffering tendencies rather than increasing them.
distractorExplanations.B: This describes the Bohr effect on oxygen binding, not the Haldane effect on CO2 transport.
distractorExplanations.D: The effect depends on hemoglobin chemistry and bicarbonate conversion, not direct displacement from plasma by oxygen.

learningObjective: Differentiate the Haldane effect from the Bohr effect and explain pulmonary carbon dioxide unloading.

subject: physiology
chapter: Chapter 41: Transport of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide in Blood and Tissue Fluids
prompt: During a steady-state measurement, a subject takes up 250 mL O2/min and exhales 200 mL CO2/min. What is the respiratory exchange ratio?
explanation: Respiratory exchange ratio is CO2 output divided by O2 uptake. Here, 200/250 = 0.80; it is a dimensionless ratio, not the absolute difference in gas volumes.

distractorExplanations.B: 1.25 reverses the definition by dividing oxygen uptake by carbon dioxide output.
distractorExplanations.C: 0.20 is the difference divided by oxygen uptake, not the CO2-to-O2 ratio.
distractorExplanations.D: 50 mL/min is the volume-rate difference and is not a dimensionless ratio.

learningObjective: Calculate respiratory exchange ratio from measured gas exchange rates.

subject: physiology
prompt: An experimental lesion removes a small rostral ventral medullary region containing spontaneously firing neurons that project to other respiratory groups. According to the text, removal of this region can abolish respiratory rhythm generation. Which region is it?

options.text: Carotid body
Parabrachial pneumotaxic center
Motor cortex controlling voluntary breathing
Pre-Botzinger complex

explanation: The pre-Botzinger complex is a key component of the medullary respiratory pattern generator. The text describes spontaneously firing neurons there and loss of rhythm after its removal, while noting that rhythm generation involves a broader network.

distractorExplanations.A: The carotid body is a peripheral chemoreceptor, not a medullary rhythm-generating region.
distractorExplanations.B: The pneumotaxic center lies in the upper pons and primarily modifies inspiratory duration.
distractorExplanations.C: Voluntary cortical control is distinct from the small ventral medullary region specified.

learningObjective: Identify the pre-Botzinger complex as a key component of respiratory rhythm generation.

subject: physiology
prompt: A stronger pneumotaxic signal causes the inspiratory ramp to switch off earlier. What breathing change is expected from this action?

options.text: Longer inspiration and a lower respiratory rate
Shorter inspiration and a tendency toward a higher respiratory rate
Continuous maximal inspiration without expiration
Loss of all sensory input from the carotid bodies

explanation: The pneumotaxic center limits the inspiratory ramp. Earlier termination shortens inspiration and the overall respiratory cycle, tending to increase respiratory rate.

distractorExplanations.A: This is the opposite of the effect of a stronger inspiratory switch-off signal.
distractorExplanations.C: Earlier switch-off limits inflation rather than sustaining maximal inspiration.
distractorExplanations.D: Pontine ramp control does not eliminate peripheral chemoreceptor afferent input.

learningObjective: Predict the effect of stronger pontine inspiratory termination signals on breathing.

subject: physiology
prompt: When an adult's lungs become markedly overinflated, pulmonary stretch receptors help terminate inspiration. Which afferent pathway carries the signals responsible for this Hering-Breuer inflation reflex?

options.text: Vagus nerves from stretch receptors in bronchi and bronchioles
Phrenic motor fibers from the diaphragm to the spinal cord
Glossopharyngeal nerves from the carotid bodies
Trigeminal nerves from the nasal mucosa

explanation: Bronchial and bronchiolar stretch receptors signal through the vagi to medullary respiratory neurons. The reflex switches off the inspiratory ramp and is mainly protective against excessive inflation in adults.

distractorExplanations.B: The specified phrenic motor pathway is not the vagal pulmonary stretch-receptor afferent pathway.
distractorExplanations.C: The inflation reflex originates in lung stretch receptors and uses vagal afferents, not the proposed carotid-body pathway.
distractorExplanations.D: The inflation reflex uses signals from pulmonary stretch receptors through the vagi, not a nasal sensory pathway.

learningObjective: Identify the afferent pathway and protective role of the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex.

subject: physiology
prompt: An acute rise in arterial PCO2 strongly stimulates central respiratory chemosensitive neurons. Why is this effect greater than that of a comparable increase in blood H+ alone?

options.text: Blood H+ readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, whereas CO2 cannot
CO2 stimulates breathing mainly by raising arterial PO2
Central chemosensitive neurons are completely insensitive to H+
CO2 crosses the blood-brain barrier readily and generates H+ in brain extracellular fluid and cerebrospinal fluid

explanation: CO2 readily reaches the brain fluids and reacts with water to generate H+, which directly excites chemosensitive neurons. Blood H+ crosses the blood-brain barrier much less readily.

distractorExplanations.A: This reverses the relative permeability of the barrier to H+ and CO2.
distractorExplanations.B: The central response is mediated chiefly by local acidification, not by an increase in arterial oxygen pressure.
distractorExplanations.C: H+ is an important direct stimulus to the central chemosensitive neurons.

learningObjective: Explain why carbon dioxide is a potent acute stimulus to central respiratory chemoreceptors.

subject: physiology
prompt: Arterial PCO2 remains elevated for several days. Its stimulatory effect on breathing becomes smaller than it was during the first few hours. Which change contributes to this attenuation?

options.text: Permanent loss of all peripheral chemoreceptors
Increased bicarbonate buffering that brings H+ near central respiratory neurons back toward normal
Failure of CO2 to cross the blood-brain barrier after the first day
A large increase in H+ next to central chemosensitive neurons

explanation: Renal bicarbonate adjustment and the slower increase in bicarbonate within brain fluids buffer H+. As the local H+ stimulus diminishes, the central ventilatory response to sustained hypercapnia is attenuated.

distractorExplanations.A: The adaptation described does not require destruction of peripheral chemoreceptors.
distractorExplanations.C: CO2 permeability of the blood-brain barrier does not cease after a day.
distractorExplanations.D: A larger local H+ stimulus would increase excitation rather than explain attenuation.

learningObjective: Explain the reduced central ventilatory response after sustained hypercapnia.

subject: physiology
prompt: A healthy person ascends to altitude and arterial PO2 falls to 55 mm Hg. If arterial PCO2 and pH are experimentally held at their baseline values, which pathway primarily increases ventilation in response to the low PO2?

options.text: Direct oxygen sensing by the pneumotaxic center alone
Inhibition of carotid-body glomus cells
Excitation of peripheral chemoreceptors, especially the carotid bodies
The pulmonary stretch-receptor inflation reflex

explanation: Markedly reduced arterial PO2 activates peripheral chemoreceptors, especially carotid bodies. Holding PCO2 and pH constant isolates the hypoxic ventilatory drive, which becomes prominent as PO2 falls into the region around and below 60 mm Hg.

distractorExplanations.A: Low oxygen has little direct ventilatory effect on the central respiratory center; the main pathway is peripheral.
distractorExplanations.B: Hypoxia activates, rather than inhibits, carotid-body signaling.
distractorExplanations.D: The inflation reflex responds to lung stretch, not directly to a reduction in arterial PO2.

learningObjective: Identify the predominant pathway for the ventilatory response to substantial arterial hypoxemia.

subject: physiology
prompt: Which nerve carries carotid-body chemoreceptor signals toward the medullary respiratory center after they pass through Hering's nerve?

options.text: Trigeminal nerve
Phrenic nerve
Vagus nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve

explanation: Carotid-body afferents travel through Hering's nerve into the glossopharyngeal nerve and then to the dorsal medullary respiratory region. Aortic-body afferents instead travel in the vagus nerves.

distractorExplanations.A: The carotid-body pathway enters the glossopharyngeal nerve, not the trigeminal nerve.
distractorExplanations.B: The phrenic nerve is not the carotid-body afferent route; those signals enter the glossopharyngeal nerve.
distractorExplanations.C: Vagal afferents serve aortic bodies; carotid-body afferents enter the glossopharyngeal nerve.

learningObjective: Distinguish the afferent pathways of carotid and aortic chemoreceptors.

subject: physiology
prompt: At the start of exercise, ventilation rises almost immediately, before arterial PCO2, PO2, or pH has changed enough to explain the response. Which mechanism best accounts for this early increase?

options.text: Anticipatory neural drive to the respiratory center accompanying motor commands
An obligatory large rise in arterial PCO2 before every exercise bout
Acute loss of the blood-brain barrier to hydrogen ions
Cessation of neural control until chemical feedback develops

explanation: The text attributes much of the immediate response to neurogenic signals reaching the respiratory center with motor commands to exercising muscles. Chemical feedback subsequently helps correct any mismatch between ventilation and metabolic demand.

distractorExplanations.B: The prompt specifies that the early response precedes a sufficient arterial CO2 change.
distractorExplanations.C: Exercise does not require a sudden loss of the blood-brain barrier to initiate ventilation.
distractorExplanations.D: Neural drive is active at onset and is the proposed explanation for the rapid increase.

learningObjective: Distinguish anticipatory neural control from later chemical fine-tuning of exercise ventilation.

subject: physiology
prompt: Following irritation of the trachea, a cough begins with inspiration and closure of the glottis. Why do the abdominal and other expiratory muscles then contract before the glottis opens?

options.text: To lower intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric pressure
To prevent any movement of foreign material when the glottis opens
To build high intrapulmonary pressure that drives rapid outward airflow when the glottis opens
To move the diaphragm downward and prolong inspiration

explanation: With the airway temporarily closed, forceful expiratory muscle contraction raises lung pressure. Sudden opening then produces the rapid outward airflow that helps expel material from the trachea and bronchi.

distractorExplanations.A: Compression against a closed glottis raises intrapulmonary pressure rather than lowering it.
distractorExplanations.B: The purpose of the resulting high-speed airflow is to move and expel foreign material.
distractorExplanations.D: Abdominal contraction pushes the diaphragm upward and contributes to forced expiration.

learningObjective: Explain the pressure-building phase of the cough reflex.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: Inhaled particles become trapped in mucus lining the bronchi. What is the usual next step in their normal mucociliary removal?

options.text: Cilia move the mucus toward the pharynx, where it can be swallowed or expelled
Cilia move the mucus distally toward the alveoli for permanent storage
Bronchial cilia transport mucus directly into pulmonary capillary blood
The mucus remains stationary until the particles dissolve in it

explanation: Cilia in the lower respiratory passages beat toward the pharynx. Their coordinated action moves mucus and trapped particles upward for swallowing or expulsion.

distractorExplanations.B: The lower-airway ciliary power stroke is toward the pharynx, not toward the alveoli.
distractorExplanations.C: Mucociliary transport occurs along the airway surface, not directly into the vascular compartment.
distractorExplanations.D: The mucus layer is actively transported by cilia; dissolution is not required for clearance.

learningObjective: Describe the direction and purpose of lower-airway mucociliary clearance.

subject: physiology
prompt: A sneeze is triggered by irritation of the nasal passageways. Which cranial nerve principally carries the initiating sensory impulses to the medulla?

options.text: Vagus nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Facial nerve
Trigeminal nerve

explanation: The sneeze reflex begins with nasal irritation, whose afferent impulses travel in the fifth cranial, or trigeminal, nerve. The resulting reflex directs a large outward airflow through the nose.

distractorExplanations.A: Vagal afferents are prominent in the cough reflex from lower respiratory passages, not the nasal sneeze pathway described.
distractorExplanations.B: The sneeze pathway described travels in the fifth cranial nerve, not the glossopharyngeal nerve.
distractorExplanations.C: The facial nerve is not the principal afferent route identified for initiation of the sneeze reflex.

learningObjective: Identify the sensory pathway initiating the sneeze reflex.

subject: physiology
prompt: A person with a severe cold can still produce sound by vibrating the vocal folds, but nasal obstruction changes the quality of the voice. Which explanation best separates these two observations?

options.text: The lips generate phonation, and nasal obstruction stops vocal-fold vibration
Laryngeal phonation is preserved, but nasal resonance is altered
The nasal cavity is the primary vibrator, and the vocal folds are only resonators
Articulation is generated only by the lungs, so nasal obstruction cannot affect voice quality

explanation: Phonation is produced by vibrating vocal folds in the larynx. The nasal passages and associated sinuses contribute resonance, so obstruction can change voice quality without abolishing laryngeal sound production.

distractorExplanations.A: The vocal folds generate phonation; the lips participate in articulation rather than serving as the primary vibrator.
distractorExplanations.C: This reverses the roles of the laryngeal vibrator and nasal resonating spaces.
distractorExplanations.D: Articulation involves the lips, tongue, and soft palate, and nasal resonance can change voice quality.

learningObjective: Distinguish laryngeal phonation, oral articulation, and nasal resonance.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: A patient with markedly slow circulation develops repeating cycles of gradually deeper breathing followed by gradually shallower breathing or apnea. How can the prolonged circulation time promote this Cheyne-Stokes pattern?

options.text: It prevents any carbon dioxide from reaching the brain
It delays delivery of changed blood gases to the respiratory center, allowing corrective ventilation to overshoot
It makes the respiratory center respond before gas changes occur in the lungs
It removes the effect of carbon dioxide on respiratory neurons permanently

explanation: A long lung-to-brain transport delay permits overventilation or underventilation to continue before the center receives the updated gas signal. This delayed negative-feedback response can oscillate between excessive and insufficient breathing.

distractorExplanations.A: Blood gases still reach the brain; their arrival is delayed rather than abolished.
distractorExplanations.C: The mechanism depends on a delayed, not anticipatory, central response to pulmonary gas changes.
distractorExplanations.D: CO2 sensitivity remains part of the oscillating control system; permanent loss of it is not required.

learningObjective: Explain how delayed blood-gas feedback can generate Cheyne-Stokes breathing.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: Which mechanism distinguishes central sleep apnea from the obstructive form described in the text?

options.text: Relaxation-related closure of an unusually narrow pharyngeal passage
Mechanical blockage from enlarged tonsils
Upper-airway compression by excess neck tissue
Transient loss of central neural drive to the ventilatory muscles

explanation: Central sleep apnea occurs when neural drive to the ventilatory muscles transiently ceases. Obstructive sleep apnea instead results from upper-airway closure or blockage, commonly involving the pharynx.

distractorExplanations.A: Pharyngeal closure during sleep is an obstructive mechanism.
distractorExplanations.B: Enlarged tonsils can mechanically narrow the airway and contribute to obstructive apnea.
distractorExplanations.C: External or soft-tissue narrowing is also an obstructive, not a central-drive, mechanism.

learningObjective: Differentiate the primary mechanisms of central and obstructive sleep apnea.

source.title: Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology

subject: physiology
prompt: After several days at altitude, a climber can maintain a larger hypoxia-driven increase in ventilation than immediately after arrival. Which adaptation discussed in the respiratory regulation chapter helps permit this increase?

options.text: Less central inhibition from the CO2 and H+ changes caused by sustained hyperventilation
Complete loss of the carotid bodies' response to hypoxia
An increase in the fraction of oxygen in the surrounding air
A progressive inability of the respiratory muscles to respond to neural signals

explanation: Initially, the CO2 loss caused by hyperventilation counteracts hypoxic stimulation. Over several days, central adaptation reduces this inhibitory influence, allowing low oxygen to drive substantially greater ventilation.

distractorExplanations.B: The peripheral hypoxic stimulus must remain effective; abolishing it would not explain greater ventilation.
distractorExplanations.C: Acclimatization is a physiological adaptation and does not increase the oxygen fraction of the ambient air.
distractorExplanations.D: Weaker responsiveness of respiratory muscles would impair rather than permit the greater ventilation.

learningObjective: Explain the ventilatory component of acclimatization to sustained hypoxia within the regulation chapter.

subject: physiology
subtopic: Physiological dead space from expired carbon dioxide
chapter: Chapter 40: Principles of Gas Exchange; Diffusion of Oxygen and Carbon Dioxide Through Respiratory Membranes
prompt: During steady breathing, arterial PCO2 is 40 mm Hg, mean mixed-expired PCO2 is 28 mm Hg, and tidal volume is 500 mL. Using the text's dead-space relationship VD/VT = (PaCO2 - PECO2)/PaCO2 and negligible inspired CO2, what is physiological dead-space volume?

options.text: 60 mL
350 mL
150 mL
200 mL

explanation: The physiological dead-space fraction is (40 - 28)/40 = 0.30. Multiplying by 500 mL gives 150 mL; PECO2 here is the mean mixed-expired value, not an end-tidal value.

distractorExplanations.A: 60 mL results from treating the 12 mm Hg difference as 12% rather than dividing it by 40 mm Hg.
distractorExplanations.B: 350 mL is the complementary, effective gas-exchanging portion of this tidal breath under the stated relationship.
distractorExplanations.D: 200 mL is not obtained from the required fraction of 0.30.

learningObjective: Calculate physiological dead space from arterial and mixed-expired carbon dioxide measurements.
